hypothesis: If Darwin's denudation argument holds, the time elapsed since the latter part of the Secondary (Mesozoic) period, i.e. since the youngest Chalk, is roughly 300 million years or more on the modern radiometrically calibrated timescale.
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. Data: the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) chronostratigraphic boundary ages as served by the Macrostrat API (defs/intervals, timescale 'international ages'), which carries the ICS chart's numeric ages in Ma. Quantities: age of the top of the Maastrichtian (= Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, the end of Chalk deposition) and age of the base of the Campanian (start of the youngest Chalk stages). SUPPORTS if the top-of-Maastrichtian age is >= 225 Ma (within 25% of 300 Myr, or older). Reported alongside: the base-of-Campanian age and the ratio of Darwin's 306.7 Myr to the measured age.
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the top-of-Maastrichtian age is < 225 Ma (Darwin's figure is off by more than 25%). MIXED is not possible for this one-number test. INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the API cannot be reached; INCONCLUSIVE (not-operationalizable) if the API does not return a Maastrichtian interval.
interpretation: Darwin's 'latter part of the Secondary period' is the Late Cretaceous, and 'since the late Chalk' is the time from the youngest Chalk Group strata (Campanian-Maastrichtian) to the present. The claim is a duration (about 300 million years, which he says is an underestimate of the time since the late Secondary) inferred from an assumed erosion rate; the test compares that duration with the radiometric timescale and does not test the erosion rate. Darwin himself withdrew the calculation in later editions. This follows the swarm thread's draft plan for this claim with the same 25% tolerance.
